name: Visual anchors follow the story

tasks.name: One-time migration: strip wardrobe from cached anchors
Wardrobe derivation mode in the anchor template
Appearance edit clears the identity anchor
UI: wardrobe field, per-location anchors, intervals, off switch
FORK.md, design doc amendments, decision log

problems.P1: Clothing baked into the identity anchor, contradicting the scene - a live prompt held both 'fitted dark blue-grey utility suit' and 'naked'
problems.P2: Editing base_attributes['appearance'] does not invalidate the cached anchor
problems.P3: Scene anchor is premise-level, so 'starship interior' persists after the party leaves the ship

decisions: Identity stays pinned; only state refreshes. Re-deriving identity on a cadence is the previous track's bug on a slower clock.
Wardrobe and permanent-change detection both ride the existing Reinforcement mechanism - no bespoke detectors. auto_update_reinforcments already refreshes on a cadence.
Scene anchors keyed by world_state.location (LLM-maintained via the world-state snapshot), not invalidated, so revisiting a location reuses its anchor.
scene.environment is a mode ('scene'/'creative'), not a place - it is not the location.
Wardrobe is a fallback suppressed by scene-supplied clothing or state. First-occurrence dedupe cannot resolve 'naked' against 'utility suit' - that is a contradiction, not a duplicate.
Migration strips clothing tokens from cached anchors in place rather than blanking and re-deriving: no LLM cost, idempotent, less surprising.

constraints.note: Two reinforcements per character means eight extra periodic LLM queries on a four-character scene. Intervals must be configurable and the feature switchable off.

risks: T8 is the risky task. An LLM asked 'did anything change?' will sometimes oblige. Guards: require a specific assertion, log every invalidation with its cause, rate-limit. Degrades to manual without taking the track with it.
T6's clothing vocabulary is the ongoing maintenance cost, exactly as the sanitiser blocklist proved to be.
